newsitem.title: JAPAN: Banks give cold shoulder to Japan hotelier - sources.
newsitem.headline: Banks give cold shoulder to Japan hotelier - sources.

text.p: A second big Japanese company, Gajoen Kanko KK, may go under this year after Japanese banks turned their backs on the troubled hotel operator, banking sources said on Tuesday.
"The banks suspended their transactions with Gajoen, retroactive to January 6, after it failed to honour promissory notes for a second time," a banking source told Reuters.
Gajoen's main transaction banks are Fuji Bank, Sakura Bank, Sumitomo Bank and Asahi Bank, according to the company's quarterly report.
Leading credit research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd reported earlier on Tuesday that Gajoen, which runs hotels and wedding halls, had become insolvent with debts of 9.88 billion yen ($80.9 million).
Gajoen said it could not make an immediate official comment.

"We have yet to confirm whether we have failed to honour promissory notes as reported because we have not received any reports from senior executives in charge of this matter," a company official told Reuters on Tuesday.
He said the company would hold an executive meeting in response to the situation and make an official comment later.

If the business failure is confirmed, Gajoen will be the second company on the Tokyo Stock Exchange's first section to fail this year, after sushi chain Kyotaru Co Ltd made an insolvency filing in late January with debts of 101.3 billion yen ($830 million).
Gajoen, established in 1948, went public in 1950.
A second failure to honour promissory notes is regarded in Japanese business practice as effectively a bankruptcy.
Corporate Japan has suffered a high rate of business failures in recent years and more pain is expected as the economy struggles to achieve solid recovery.

Last year saw some of the biggest bankruptcies in the postwar period as companies sank under the weight of debts left over from the free-wheeling "bubble" era of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s.

Total debts held by firms which went bust in 1996 fell 12.1 percent from the previous year to 8.12 trillion yen ($66.5 billion), but it was still the third-highest figure on record, Tokyo Commerce and Industry Research Co reported last month.
Gajoen shares were suspended by the Tokyo Stock Exchange for the whole of Tuesday's afternoon session. The shares were last traded at 66 yen in the morning.
The shares were put under surveillance by the exchange last September after the hotel operator said it had overdue taxes totalling about 13 billion yen ($106 million).
Teikoku Databank said the company expanded its business to real estate transactions and posted annual revenues of 1.55 billion yen ($12.7 million) in the year to February 1990.

But its financial condition worsened in the early 1990s, when the bubble burst, partly on its inability to collect some loans. In 1995/96, revenue slumped, with uncovered losses soaring to more than five billion yen ($40.9 million).
Last November, Gajoen said it saw a net loss of 5.3 billion yen ($43.4 million) for the year to February 28, after an actual net loss of 94 million yen ($770,000) the year before. ($1=122 yen)
